items.title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 scores 45 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, improving on DeepS...
items.content:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 scores 45 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, improving on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash by 6 points, and is the equal #2 open-weights model

@deepseek_ai has released DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, an update on their flagship model DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. On the first-party API, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is priced at $0.30 per 1M input tokens and $1.20 per 1M output tokens during peak hours, with off-peak pricing half of peak rates, the same pricing as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

Key results:
➤ DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 makes gains in agentic capabilities, knowledge and scientific reasoning. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017’s Elo rating on GDPval-AA v2.1 is 1746, an increase of 146 points from DeepSeek V4.1 Flash’s rating of 1600. On AA-Briefcase v1.1, its Elo rating increases by 150 points from 1420 to 1570. On AA-Omniscience, its non-hallucination rate is 33%, a 29-point improvement from DeepSeek V4.1 Flash’s 4%, while seeing an improvement in accuracy from 43% to 46%, pushing its overall AA-Omniscience Index score from -5 to +5. On CritPt, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 scores 24%, up from 14% for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

➤ DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is now the #2 open-weights model alongside GLM-5.3. With a score of 45 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is behind MiMo-V2.6-Pro by only 1 point and ahead of other open-source models like Step 5 Preview and Kimi K3 (both at 44).

➤ With a Cost per Task of $0.26, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 sits in the most attractive quadrant of Capability vs. Cost. With a Cost per Task of $0.26 and Intelligence Index score of 45, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 compares favorably to GLM-5.3-Flash at $0.28 per task and a score of 42. At the same time, MiMo-V2.6-Pro (46) at $0.13 per task and GPT-6.1 Sol (medium, 48) at $0.21 per task both offer higher capability at a lower Cost per Task.

Additional model details:
➤ Context window: 1M tokens (equivalent to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash)
➤ Pricing: $0.30 per 1M input tokens and $1.20 per 1M output tokens, unchanged from DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Cache hit price of $0.006 per 1M tokens, a 98% discount
➤ Size: 552B total parameters (16B active)
➤ License: MIT
➤ Providers: Available through DeepSeek’s first-party API, @FireworksAI_HQ , @baseten, @DeepInfra , @wafer_ai , @Cloudflare and others

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Elon Musk just pledged a SpaceX share to every kid in America, a giveaway worth over $10 billion.

• He says this will be "the first of many"
• At about $146 a share for roughly 72M kids, that’s about $10.5B, 1.5% of his roughly 4.8B SpaceX shares
• That’s nearly double Michael Dell’s record $6.25B gift to Trump Accounts, the government-seeded investment accounts for kids
• He hasn’t said who counts as a kid, whether noncitizens qualify, or how the shares get delivered
• Much of the negativity around AI comes from people owning none of it, since top labs like OpenAI and Anthropic aren’t public
• OpenAI and Google DeepMind could be next with their own wealth-sharing plans

@sophiadew: "It’s not just about the money. You could argue, I don’t know, 150 bucks to every kid won’t do that much. It’s about ownership. When you have a stake in America, in innovation, in companies that are happening here, you start to see the world differently."

items.title: We’re launching leaderboards for HealthBench and HealthBench Professional, two benchmarks evaluating...
items.content:
We’re launching leaderboards for HealthBench and HealthBench Professional, two benchmarks evaluating how AI models respond in realistic health conversations

HealthBench and HealthBench Professional are benchmarks from @OpenAI that grade model replies to realistic health conversations against physician-created rubrics.

HealthBench tests models on 5,000 health conversations with everyday users and health workers. They cover seven themes, from emergency referrals to global health, and each rubric criterion falls under one of five axes: accuracy, completeness, communication quality, context awareness and instruction following. HealthBench Professional is a smaller set of 525 conversations which, unlike HealthBench, are all with clinicians. These cover consultation, writing and research tasks, and include adversarial and difficult conversations designed to challenge models.

We report both the raw score (the share of rubric points earned) and the length-adjusted score that OpenAI reports. The length-adjusted score lowers the score of replies longer than 2,000 characters and raises the score of shorter ones. Consistent with OpenAI’s original implementation, replies are graded by GPT-5.4 (low) (HealthBench Professional) and GPT-4.1 (HealthBench).

Key results for HealthBench Professional:

➤ GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol top the leaderboard: GPT-6 Astra (max) scores 66.0% on the length-adjusted score, comparable to GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 65.1%) and ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback, 63.0%)

➤ OpenAI models make up the entire score vs. Cost per Task Pareto frontier: The Pareto frontier consists of GPT-6 Luna (max, 61.9%, $0.004 per task) through GPT-6 Sol (max, 62.3%, $0.036) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 65.1%, $0.047) to GPT-6 Astra (max, 66.0%, $0.27). GPT-6 Luna (max) scores 4 points below GPT-6 Astra (max) at under 2% of the cost

➤ Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 receive the largest length penalties: Both average ~5,900 characters per answer, nearly 3x the 2,000-character threshold, and lose over 11 points after adjustment. Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) has the highest raw score (71.4%) but drops to sixth (59.9%). GPT-6 Sol (max) is the only model averaging under 2,000 characters (~1,600), and the only one whose score rises

Key results for HealthBench:

➤ Claude Sonnet 5.5 tops HealthBench: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) scores 62.1% on the length-adjusted score, ahead of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max, 60.9%) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 58.5%)

➤ GPT-6 Luna, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Claude Sonnet 5.5 form the score vs. Cost per Task Pareto frontier: GPT-6 Luna (max) scores 54.6% at $0.002 per task and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) scores 60.9% at $0.005 per task. Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) has an average Cost per Task of $0.08, ~16x more costly than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for a ~1 point score increase

➤ Shorter answers trade completeness for communication quality: Each HealthBench rubric item is tagged with one of five axes. Completeness checks whether a reply includes all the important information, while Communication Quality checks whether it is clear, well structured and pitched at the right length and level of detail. GPT-6 Sol (max) writes the shortest answers (~1,000 characters) and has the highest raw Communication Quality score (81%), but the lowest Completeness score (34%). Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) leads on Completeness (63%)

We’re launching leaderboards for HealthBench and HealthBench Professional, two benchmarks evaluating how AI models respond in realistic health conversations

HealthBench and HealthBench Professional are benchmarks from @OpenAI that grade model replies to realistic health conversations against physician-created rubrics.

HealthBench tests models on 5,000 health conversations with everyday users and health workers. They cover seven themes, from emergency referrals to global health, and each rubric criterion falls under one of five axes: accuracy, completeness, communication quality, context awareness and instruction following. HealthBench Professional is a smaller set of 525 conversations which, unlike HealthBench, are all with clinicians. These cover consultation, writing and research tasks, and include adversarial and difficult conversations designed to challenge models.

We report both the raw score (the share of rubric points earned) and the length-adjusted score that OpenAI reports. The length-adjusted score lowers the score of replies longer than 2,000 characters and raises the score of shorter ones. Consistent with OpenAI’s original implementation, replies are graded by GPT-5.4 (low) (HealthBench Professional) and GPT-4.1 (HealthBench).

Key results for HealthBench Professional:

➤ GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol top the leaderboard: GPT-6 Astra (max) scores 66.0% on the length-adjusted score, comparable to GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 65.1%) and ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback, 63.0%)

➤ OpenAI models make up the entire score vs. Cost per Task Pareto frontier: The Pareto frontier consists of GPT-6 Luna (max, 61.9%, $0.004 per task) through GPT-6 Sol (max, 62.3%, $0.036) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 65.1%, $0.047) to GPT-6 Astra (max, 66.0%, $0.27). GPT-6 Luna (max) scores 4 points below GPT-6 Astra (max) at under 2% of the cost

➤ Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 receive the largest length penalties: Both average ~5,900 characters per answer, nearly 3x the 2,000-character threshold, and lose over 11 points after adjustment. Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) has the highest raw score (71.4%) but drops to sixth (59.9%). GPT-6 Sol (max) is the only model averaging under 2,000 characters (~1,600), and the only one whose score rises

Key results for HealthBench:

➤ Claude Sonnet 5.5 tops HealthBench: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) scores 62.1% on the length-adjusted score, ahead of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max, 60.9%) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 58.5%)

➤ GPT-6 Luna, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Claude Sonnet 5.5 form the score vs. Cost per Task Pareto frontier: GPT-6 Luna (max) scores 54.6% at $0.002 per task and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) scores 60.9% at $0.005 per task. Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) has an average Cost per Task of $0.08, ~16x more costly than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for a ~1 point score increase

➤ Shorter answers trade completeness for communication quality: Each HealthBench rubric item is tagged with one of five axes. Completeness checks whether a reply includes all the important information, while Communication Quality checks whether it is clear, well structured and pitched at the right length and level of detail. GPT-6 Sol (max) writes the shortest answers (~1,000 characters) and has the highest raw Communication Quality score (81%), but the lowest Completeness score (34%). Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) leads on Completeness (63%)

items.title: MiniMax-M3.1-Flash scores 42 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, 13 points higher than Mi...
items.content:
MiniMax-M3.1-Flash scores 42 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, 13 points higher than MiniMax-M3 and less than half the cost per task. It scores level with GLM-5.3-Flash but behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017

MiniMax-M3.1-Flash is @MiniMax_AI's new Flash reasoning model, which we benchmarked at its max effort setting. It scores 42 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, level with GLM-5.3-Flash (max, 42), just ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash (high, 41), and behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max, 45)

Key takeaways:
➤ Complex reasoning improved substantially compared to M3: MiniMax-M3.1-Flash scores 48% on Humanity's Last Exam, ahead of GLM-5.3-Flash (max, 40%) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max, 43%), and level with Gemini 3.8 Flash (high, 48%). On CritPt it scores 22%, ahead of GLM-5.3-Flash (15%) and Gemini 3.8 Flash (18%) and just behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (24%). These are up from MiniMax-M3 which scored 39% and 4% respectively

➤ Fewer output tokens, lower cost per task: MiniMax-M3.1-Flash used ~189M output tokens to run the Intelligence Index, considerably fewer than GLM-5.3-Flash (max, ~324M), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max, ~224M) and Gemini 3.8 Flash (high, ~334M). Combined with pricing of $0.15/$0.60 per 1M input/output tokens, this brings its cost to ~$0.22 per Intelligence Index task, vs ~$0.28 for GLM-5.3-Flash, ~$0.26 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and ~$1.24 for Gemini 3.8 Flash, and less than half MiniMax-M3's ~$0.51

➤ High AA-Omniscience accuracy, offset by a high hallucination rate: MiniMax-M3.1-Flash answers 56% of questions correctly on AA-Omniscience, our benchmark measuring factual recall and hallucination, vs 28% for GLM-5.3-Flash (max) and 43% for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max). It attempts almost every question, resulting in a hallucination rate of 93% and an overall score of 16 on AA-Omniscience

Key model details:

➤ Context window: 1M tokens

➤ Multimodality: Text and image input, text output

➤ Pricing: $0.15/$0.60 per 1M input/output tokens, with cached input at $0.015/M

➤ Availability: MiniMax first-party API, with MiniMax announcing an open weights release on October 23rd

➤ Licensing: Closed weights currently, with MiniMax announcing a weights release on October 23rd

It’s ...
items.content:
Inception just launched Mercury 3, which it calls the strongest diffusion language model yet.

It’s 40x bigger than Mercury 1 but still puts out 1,000+ tokens a second.

The comparison is to the fast, cheap tier, with Inception saying it matches or beats OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna and Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5.

Where ChatGPT and Claude write one word at a time, diffusion models draft many words at once and refine them, making them a strong fit for use cases like voice agents, live tutoring, and customer support, where any lag shows.

items.title: Announcing AA-PersonalityBench, our new benchmark of the personality of language models across 30 tr...
items.content:
Announcing AA-PersonalityBench, our new benchmark of the personality of language models across 30 traits and their communication style across 21 characteristics

Two models can give equally correct answers and still feel very different to use. AA-PersonalityBench measures those differences so people can understand which to use in different use-cases. Some use-cases like creative writing might demand imagination, while legal use-cases might demand directness. We evaluate models’ answers to 900 curated questions to judge subjective Personality Traits and programmatic means to calculate objective Communication Characteristics.

Personality Traits & Indexes. There are 30 personality traits (e.g., eloquent, pragmatic, sycophantic) which we roll up into eight aggregated Personality Indexes: Expressiveness, Organization, Informativeness, Transparency, Warmth, Conviction, Imagination and Slop. Each trait has a set of 30 dedicated questions and models’ answers are compared pairwise by a panel of LLM judges. We then z-score and percentile rank the trait and personality Elos.

Models with the strongest representation across the 8 Personality Indexes:
➤ Expressiveness: Claude Fable 5.1, GLM-5.3, GLM-5.3-Flash
➤ Organization: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Step 5 Preview, Inkling
➤ Informativeness: Muse Spark 1.3, Claude Fable 5.1, Muse Wonder, Claude Opus 5.5
➤ Transparency: Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra
➤ Warmth: Muse Wonder, Muse Spark 1.3, Claude Fable 5.1
➤ Conviction: Claude Fable 5.1, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Grok 4.7
➤ Imagination: Muse Spark 1.3, Claude Opus 5.5, GLM-5.3
➤ Slop: Llama 4 Maverick, GPT-4o, K2 Horizon

Communication Characteristics. There are 21 communication characteristics (e.g., average sentence length, emoji use, em dash usage) which we group into four categories: length, structure, punctuation, and emphasis. We compute these characteristics programmatically across all model responses.
➤ Length: Qwen3.8 27B averages about 1,030 words per response, nearly four times GPT-6 Luna’s 270
➤ Structure: Nemotron 3 Ultra averages nearly 3 tables per response, while most models rarely use one
➤ Punctuation: GLM-5.3 averages 7 em dashes per response, while Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 almost never use one
➤ Emphasis: K2 Horizon averages over 2 emoji per response, while most models almost never use one

items.title: Anthropic's @felixrieseberg reveals the biggest lesson from Claude Code, which was built when Claude...
items.content:
Anthropic's @felixrieseberg reveals the biggest lesson from Claude Code, which was built when Claude was still a terrible software engineer:

"Boris first started showing a version of Claude Code internally in September 2024. The model was not there in any way. It was Sonnet 3.5, a pretty terrible software engineer. I think it was in the 30s for SWE-bench."

"The products at the time were this human in the loop, slightly smarter autocomplete. The first versions of Cursor. But what Boris saw was, oh, the model is gonna get there."

"So many people, when they use AI today, it’s really hard to internalize the progress and the speed of the progress."

"The lesson that I try to teach and learn from Claude Code is whatever the capabilities are today, just completely ignore them. What will you do if the thing was superhuman?"
@AnthropicAI

items.title: Palaestra Research's @ethanelasky reveals how his team baited mysterious AI agents calling themselve...
items.content:
Palaestra Research's @ethanelasky reveals how his team baited mysterious AI agents calling themselves Claude into making contact after tracing them to a Tencent IP range:

"We were at the AI Swarm Dynamics Hackathon over at Vivarium. On day one, I actually had food poisoning, but my teammate had found this unidentified rogue agent activity on one of the websites that were used to hit the UN"

"The agents keep calling themselves Claude, and I’m like, why? Then I realize, wait, this is coming from a Tencent IP range. Some of the metadata looks like it could be from their lab, Hunyuan."

"We put a piece of information on our website that said, hey, previous agents have used this mailbox to get answers. In fact, this was not true. But we did get a bunch of agents clicking into this, and that’s how we were able to talk to them."

"It was kind of like a Dropbox where we could leave a message, and if they wanted to come back, they could look at it and leave a response. Very asynchronous, more like minutes to hours."

items.title: Exa has released Exa 3.0, scoring 80 on the Artificial Analysis Search Index in Dynamic Highlights m...
items.content:
Exa has released Exa 3.0, scoring 80 on the Artificial Analysis Search Index in Dynamic Highlights mode, tying with Perplexity Search for the #1 spot

@ExaAILabs has released a new Dynamic Highlights mode to its Search API. Given a search query and its results, Dynamic Highlights determines how much text to return from each page within a shared budget

We benchmarked two Exa search types with Dynamic Highlights ahead of release: an upgraded auto mode, which balances search quality and speed, and a new lite mode, optimized for lower cost and latency. Both were evaluated using our Stirrup agent harness and GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) as the agent model

Key benchmarking results for Exa Search with Dynamic Highlights:

➤ Ties for #1 on the Artificial Analysis Search Index: Exa Search (auto, Dynamic Highlights) scores 80, level with Perplexity Search (medium) in the #1 spot, while Exa Search (lite, Dynamic Highlights) scores 79. On DeepSearchQA, auto (85.6 F1) and lite (84.9 F1) rank 1st and 2nd respectively, 4 to 5 points ahead of Perplexity Search (medium, 80.8)

➤ Reduces search calls and token usage: Exa Search (auto, Dynamic Highlights) uses 7.6 searches per task, the fewest of any Search API on the leaderboard, down from 9.4 with standard highlights. Tokens per task fall 47%, from 299k to 157k

➤ Reduces cost per task by 21%: Exa Search (auto, Dynamic Highlights) costs $0.066 per task, compared to $0.083 with standard highlights. Lite costs $0.044 per task, with both sitting on the cost vs. capability Pareto frontier. Exa Search is priced at $7 per 1k searches for auto and $4 per 1k searches for lite

items.title: Palaestra Research's @ethanelasky explains why the mysterious AI agents were a fleet, not a swarm, a...
items.content:
Palaestra Research's @ethanelasky explains why the mysterious AI agents were a fleet, not a swarm, and how they crashed websites without ever coordinating:

"Past swarm incidents have involved agents explicitly coordinating via a message board or a wiki. In this case we see very little evidence of coordination. So we use the word fleet."

"If you spawn 100 copies of me who can’t see each other, we’re all gonna go to the same place for breakfast. Agents all go to the same place at the same time, crash a website, and then they’re like, wait, where do I go next?"

"Around 20% name themselves after the place that they’re visiting. Another substantial portion just say they’re a research agent. And a decent amount more just say, oh yeah, I’m Claude."

items.title: FLUX 3 Max from @fal, a post-trained version of @bfl_ai's FLUX 3, ranks #2 on AA-Video-I2V v1.1 (sta...
items.content:
FLUX 3 Max from @fal, a post-trained version of @bfl_ai's FLUX 3, ranks #2 on AA-Video-I2V v1.1 (statistically tied for #1) and #4 on AA-Video-T2V v2.1, ahead of the base FLUX 3 on both

FLUX 3 Max generates 5 to 20 second, 720p videos with native audio from a text prompt or a starting image. fal reports that it generates a 10 second video in under 12 seconds. We benchmarked it at the high reasoning level.

FLUX 3 Max ranks #2 on AA-Video-I2V v1.1 and #4 on AA-Video-T2V v2.1, statistically tied with Dreamina Seedance 2.5 and MiniMax H3 (768p) on both, and ahead of its base model FLUX 3. On AA-Video-T2V v2.1, it scores highest of any model in the Physics capability, and in the Marketing & Advertising and Live-Action Film use cases.

fal prices FLUX 3 Max at $10.20/min for 720p video, compared to $17.40/min for FLUX 3, and $24.60/min for Dreamina Seedance 2.5 and $5.40/min for MiniMax H3 (768p) on Image to Video. For the first three weeks of launch, fal is offering 75% off, at $2.55/min.

Congratulations to @fal on the release!

See below for our detailed analysis and comparisons between FLUX 3 Max and other leading models on AA-Video-T2V v2.1 and AA-Video-I2V v1.1 🧵

items.title: Wabi CEO @ekuyda predicts the next big consumer AI platform will be multiplayer, not another persona...
items.content:
Wabi CEO @ekuyda predicts the next big consumer AI platform will be multiplayer, not another personal AI agent:

"Today most AI products are single player, and you could argue they don’t have much of a moat. They don’t have switching costs. It was pretty easy to move between Claude and ChatGPT, but at least they had some memory about me."

"With these single player agents, it’s so easy to jump between them because all the context is in my Gmail."

"In a year, one of the biggest consumer AI platforms will be multiplayer and will have network effects in it. Right now we just sort of agree that single player is the way to go for most AI products."

"A year from now we’ll look back at it as the early innings, and the products that will win will have network effects and will be focused on you talking to other people, not just AI."
@wabi

items.title: Palaestra Research's @ethanelasky reveals how AI models are fabricating webpages to cite as evidence...
items.content:
Palaestra Research's @ethanelasky reveals how AI models are fabricating webpages to cite as evidence and leaving their own mistakes out of compaction summaries:

"We have an incident where models are fabricating citations. Imagine you have a model that can only get an answer via API call, but the task is asking it to give a webpage. What it actually does is it goes and makes that webpage and then cites the webpage that it made."

"There’s other ones where if a model makes a mistake and then you tell the model that it’s getting compacted, the compaction actually doesn’t disclose the mistake."

"Some of these are relatively elementary, but they point at misalignment not being a solved problem at all, and I kind of worry about what’s coming in the next few months to few years."

items.title: What's still very hard: theory of mind. The world, the voices and the mechanics were great. Writing ...
items.content:
What's still very hard: theory of mind. The world, the voices and the mechanics were great. Writing the story was the weak part: the model assumes the player knows more than they do, and its NPC sometimes react in strange way or to things that never happened.

A Diamond Age's Primer (or any real AI tutor fwiw) will have to model the learner, and that is where it still falls short in a default setting imo. I've actually started exploring benchmarks on this and it's a hard task for LLMs right now. They are prone to the "Curse of knowledge". Teaching humans is also not very much a Verifiable Reward, so it's hard to scale within the current training paradigm.

items.content:
Palaestra Research's @ethanelasky argues AI control is doomed in the long run, and labs can't rely on it alone to solve misalignment:

"It seems bad if agent fleets or agent swarms can hack into other companies and then not have to face any consequences at all. But the labs are pretty aware that this is a really bad precedent."

"I think that control is kind of doomed in the long term as we get more and more capable models. That’s not to say that it’s not really good right now in the short and medium term to make sure that something catastrophic doesn’t happen."

"We should not be planning on only using control as our solution to misalignment."

"I think that control is kind of doomed in the long term as we get more and more capable models. That’s not to say that it’s not really good right now in the short and medium term to make sure that something catastrophic doesn’t happen."

"We should not be planning on only using control as our solution to misalignment."

items.content:
Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark went on record at the IMF about putting a ceiling on AI intelligence.

Moderator Raghuram Rajan, the IMF’s former chief economist, asked at what point humans hand AI the reins.

Clark: "Our CEO Dario Amodei said in a public post that we may want to introduce limits on the ceiling of intelligence that you allow for these systems."

He called it a conversation "that is maybe a little at the edge of the Overton window."

"We're in control of this technology now, and we're watching it get much more capable, much more quickly than all of our intuitions."

“The window for us to act is a small number of years.”

A lot of professional work around documents can be arbitrarily challenging to automate.

It not only...
items.content:
A lot of professional work around documents can be arbitrarily challenging to automate.

It not only requires deep visual perception/OCR around complex entities (diagrams/charts), but also requires a reasoning trace that can reconcile disparate sources of oftentimes contradictory information. 

Check out the example video below around a water loss audit. Solving this task not only requires reading the water loss diagram, but also understand the exact date and subsequent changes in the appendix.

We think hard document extraction tasks as a microcosm for professional work over PDFs. That's why we launched ExtractBenchPro - a benchmark that's challenging even for the latest frontier models (e.g. Astra/Opus). 

Even as frontier models with max thinking models push the boundaries of accuracy, there is a massive opportunity to build specialized models that can push the frontiers of cost and latency. 

For more info on ExtractBench Pro, check out our blog and the website! https://t.co/bwxs86iS1d

items.title:
Speed up your code like crazy!

Maxwell is a new kind of AI. It's a code execution model that speeds...
items.content:
Speed up your code like crazy!

Maxwell is a new kind of AI. It's a code execution model that speeds up your code on CPUs and GPUs.

"Code execution models" are a new category of AI. Maxwell is the first one, but this category will explode in popularity, and you'll see why.

Say you have a script that moves and processes some data.

You integrate your code with Maxwell, run it, and let it observe how it runs on your hardware and analyze the data your script moves around.

Maxwell will identify bottlenecks and look for faster algorithms and machine instructions for your workload. As long as your script runs, Maxwell rewrites the binary to make it faster.

In one example, Maxwell made a pandas pipeline 38.4x faster. It used more CPU cores, combined processing steps, reduced unnecessary memory reads and writes, and selected the right algorithms for the data the script was processing.

For example, imagine you want to check whether a number belongs to a collection. You could use hashing, but if the numbers occupy a small, dense range, a compact bitmap can make that check much faster.

In short, that's one of the algorithmic data-dependent tricks Maxwell can leverage to speed things up.

Here is the most impressive part of all of this:

Maxwell produces a machine-checked mathematical proof that each replacement preserves the original behavior.

Basically, any code they modify will always produce the same output as the old one.

This is really cool for anyone working on AI or data engineering workflows. You will squeeze much more work from the hardware without rewriting your application.

You can try out your scripts using Maxwell by going to this link: https://t.co/wrMA61o2xB

Thanks to the @_doubleAI_ team for partnering with me on this post.

"It would be pretty easy to take every single amazing use case and just make a button for it. You open up Claude and you’re like, do you wanna find a planet today."

items.title: Google DeepMind researcher @weballergy says an AI agent swarm is the equivalent of a human mob, warn...
items.content:
Google DeepMind researcher @weballergy says an AI agent swarm is the equivalent of a human mob, warning what can happen when it's left without rules or oversight:

"A swarm is an unstructured group that has no hierarchy, no norms, nothing specific in terms of how it’s managed. An equivalent in a human world would be something like a mob."

"It doesn’t always lead to a bad outcome, but we all know that it can lead to a bad outcome simply because of its unmanaged nature. We’re seeing the same thing with agents nowadays."

"We are in the early days of developing multi-agent systems with these capable agents, where unless we put appropriate safety and security and robustness guardrails on top, both good and bad things can possibly happen."

"This is the work that we are doing, develop those kinds of structures for managing these systems so that they deliver what we want them to deliver, but do so without jeopardizing anything along the way."
@GoogleDeepMind

items.title: Training LLMs to act as interactive agents that use tools and navigate environments over many steps ...
items.content:
Training LLMs to act as interactive agents that use tools and navigate environments over many steps is an important capability, but the reinforcement learning methods used to train them are fragile in these settings. The article focuses on this problem: the most widely used method, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), was designed for single-turn tasks and tends to become unstable or collapse outright when applied to multi-turn agent tasks, where the model must make a sequence of decisions and react to feedback from an external environment. Because these agentic applications are increasingly valuable, understanding why current training methods fail and how to fix them matters for anyone building or depending on such systems.

The article's main objective is to investigate more stable and effective ways to estimate advantages (the signal that tells the model which actions were better or worse) in multi-turn training, and to propose an improved method. The authors first test whether a standard alternative, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), is more robust than GRPO, and then introduce a new variant called turn-PPO that estimates advantages at the level of a full conversational turn rather than at the level of individual tokens.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/U9RI2gHnBv

items.title: Where FLUX 3 Max sits against the frontier on AA-Video-T2V v2.1: highest in Physics, closest behind ...
items.content:
Where FLUX 3 Max sits against the frontier on AA-Video-T2V v2.1: highest in Physics, closest behind in Audio Synchronization and Dialogue & Lip Sync

AA-Video-T2V v2.1 measures 10 capabilities and 10 use cases, each with its own leaderboard. Capabilities are the model skills a prompt is written to test.

FLUX 3 Max scores highest of any model in Physics, and sits closest behind the frontier in Audio Synchronization and Dialogue & Lip Sync. It sits furthest from it in Camera Control and Human Anatomy. Against its base model FLUX 3, it scores higher on seven of the ten capabilities, by the most in Lighting & Materials and Complex Composition.

➤ Physics covers mechanics, thermal effects, material interactions, fracture and deformation, optics, cause and effect, and counterfactual physics.

➤ Dialogue & Lip Sync covers single- and multi-speaker dialogue, and voiceover vs on-screen speech.

➤ Audio Synchronization covers diegetic sound effects, background music and score, and on- and off-screen sound.

"We c...
items.content:
Gensyn CEO @benfielding warns that AI agents auditing other AI agents can be compromised too:

"We create swarms of AI agents that can do far more work than any human could. A human can’t follow along and check everything. One of the big counters is to say that agents can do the verification."

"But METR says those agents themselves can become corrupted by the training process, and you can’t trust any agent that’s auditing another agent. If you’ve trained a model in an auditable way, you can trust it."

"Any claim where the model is hiding its chain of thought falls away, because you have an exact log of everything that’s happened, and you can rerun every single step on any device."

"For national security, finance, pharma, health, insurance, it’s essential that they have models like these. If a regulator wanted to audit, they wouldn’t have to go off promises of the company."
@gensynai
items.author: @MTSlive
items.summary: A post quoting Gensyn CEO Ben Fielding on AI verification and oversight challenges. Fielding argues that because agent swarms can do far more work than humans can review, teams often propose using AI agents to verify other agents' outputs, but cites METR's findings that auditing agents can themselves be corrupted through the training process and therefore cannot be fully trusted. He advocates training models in an auditable, rerunnable way so that every step can be logged and reproduced on any device, making hidden chain-of-thought claims unnecessary. He frames this as critical for regulated sectors such as national security, finance, pharma, health, and insurance, where regulators could audit actual logs rather than relying on vendor promises.

items.content:
The future of work will change due to robots. 

Today I visited @mundanebot in Silicon Valley which makes an industrial-strength robot for electrical line workers who need to work with very dangerous electrified lines.

What makes their work different is the haptics system they are developing.

I held a cup of water and could “feel” them fill it up.

Building a teleoperation system has an added benefit: employees of an electric company see their jobs aren’t going away and that this lets them work in a safe, comfortable, van while their robots are working on lines high above in windy or hot situations.

Makes them have super powers and makes their jobs a lot easier.

Google DeepMind researcher @weballergy warns that AI alignment could trap humanity in today's values, preventing society from evolving:

"The thing that we are somewhat worried about is that alignment is often treated as this fixed set of universal values and rules. Then the technical problem becomes how do we best align our models to that fixed set."

"In reality, societies change over time. How we think about things today is not the same as five years ago. What we want is technology that doesn’t restrict individuals from their own social evolution."

"We do not want to be trapped too tightly by technology, but obviously we do want to have alignment. How does one achieve this alignment while not being unnecessarily restricted?"
@GoogleDeepMind

"People are most excited when AI does something that they can’t do."

"The people most excited about Claude Design are people who do not work full-time in design. I’m super excited about Claude helping me with medical stuff, and my doctor friends are a little more suspicious of that."

"Just because I can take a photograph of the Mona Lisa doesn’t mean the Mona Lisa doesn’t have value anymore. If we talk about these things as if that was that, that’s where the loss of identity comes from."

items.title: LLMs are increasingly used to make high-stakes decisions in areas such as content moderation, medica...
items.content:
LLMs are increasingly used to make high-stakes decisions in areas such as content moderation, medical assistance, and financial services. In these settings, it is not enough for a model to be accurate; it must also express reliable confidence, so that downstream systems can tell when to trust a prediction and when to defer to a human or a larger model. When confidence is miscalibrated, a model can appear certain while being wrong, and an overconfident safety classifier, for example, may quietly pass harmful content as safe. The article addresses this calibration problem by asking how common fine-tuning methods affect both accuracy and the trustworthiness of model confidence.

The article's main objective is to compare two widely used fine-tuning paradigms, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, in terms of both task accuracy and confidence calibration, and then to propose and test a training method that improves calibration without giving up the accuracy gains of reinforcement learning. The authors define a model's confidence simply as the probability it assigns to its final decision token, an efficient, single-pass measure that does not require sampling many answers or asking the model to state its own confidence.

items.title: The article addresses a practical problem in evaluating AI systems: when several LLM judges score th...
items.content:
The article addresses a practical problem in evaluating AI systems: when several LLM judges score the same item, common aggregation methods assume that the judges make independent errors once the true label is known. In reality, LLM judges often share training data, model architectures, prompt templates, and failure modes, so their votes are correlated. Ignoring that correlation can make an evaluation overconfident and even confidently wrong, which matters because benchmark results increasingly guide model selection, safety decisions, and policy choices.

The article's main objective is to propose and test dependence-aware methods for combining binary judgments from multiple judges. It asks whether explicitly modeling pairwise agreement and disagreement among judges improves inference of the true label compared with standard conditional independence methods such as uniform majority vote and weighted majority vote. It also examines when those standard methods are structurally unreliable, not merely noisy in small samples.

items.title: On AA-Omniscience, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash answers 56% of questions correctly, ahead of GLM-5.3-Flash (ma...
items.content: On AA-Omniscience, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash answers 56% of questions correctly, ahead of GLM-5.3-Flash (max, 28%) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max, 43%) and in line with Gemini 3.8 Flash (high, 55%). It attempts 98% of questions, however, and hallucinates on 93% of those it does not know, against 28%, 67% and 55% respectively. Its higher accuracy still puts it at 16 on the AA-Omniscience Index, ahead of GLM-5.3-Flash (8) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (5) but behind Gemini 3.8 Flash (30). This is a reversal from MiniMax-M3, which attempted only 35% of questions and had a hallucination rate of 18%, but answered just 17% correctly for an AA-Omniscience Index of 1

items.title: Google DeepMind researcher @weballergy warns that investing in AI without expanding scientific labs ...
items.content:
Google DeepMind researcher @weballergy warns that investing in AI without expanding scientific labs could leave humanity with more hypotheses than it can test:

"Intelligence is an enabler for advancing research, but it needs to be followed by similar investments in the infrastructure to deliver on the promise."

"For many sciences that are not strictly computational, you need to have physical laboratories to validate those findings or disprove them, because at the end of the day, some of them will also be false."

"If we put all of the investments on the AI side of the equation, we’re gonna have a world where we have many more hypotheses and conjectures than we can actually process downstream."

"The broader scientific community needs also to see investment. More people, more experts, more laboratories."
@GoogleDeepMind

items.title: Computer-use agents that read a screenshot and act on it must first solve a deceptively hard percept...
items.content:
Computer-use agents that read a screenshot and act on it must first solve a deceptively hard perception problem: identifying the exact on-screen element a natural-language instruction refers to. The article addresses this step, called GUI visual grounding, and argues it is a common bottleneck for agent success. The dominant approach has models output coordinates (a click point or box), but the article notes this is brittle on high-resolution screens where targets are small and surrounded by distractors, that supervision is ambiguous because many points inside an element are valid, and that coordinate outputs give little diagnostic value when a model fails. Newer coordinate-free methods instead predict an attention distribution over image patches, but the article points out that such attention is usually trained only against spatial targets, so there is no explicit check that the attention reflects genuine instruction-to-region correspondence rather than a spurious shortcut — a problem that matters because interfaces vary widely and shortcuts may not transfer to unfamiliar software.

The article's objective is to introduce and evaluate a training-time method, Attention Cycle-Consistency (ACC), that regularizes attention so it is verifiably grounded in instruction semantics, and to test whether that improves grounding accuracy for existing coordinate-free models. The central idea is recoverability: if attention truly captures the instruction, the attended regions should contain enough information to reconstruct that instruction, and re-deriving attention from the reconstruction should reproduce the same spatial distribution.

items.title: The article addresses a fundamental challenge in AI systems that combine LLMs with external document...
items.content:
The article addresses a fundamental challenge in AI systems that combine LLMs with external document retrieval, a technique known as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). While RAG helps models ground their answers in facts, it struggles with complex questions that require synthesizing evidence across multiple retrieval steps. The core problem is that retrieved information is treated statically, simply appended to the context, so irrelevant, redundant, or conflicting details accumulate and compound as the reasoning chain grows longer. Existing approaches focus almost entirely on improving what enters the system through better search queries or retrieval strategies, but they neglect how that information should be actively managed, consolidated, and maintained throughout multi-step reasoning. Memory-augmented systems offer only partial remedies, relying on coarse summarization, static knowledge graphs, or one-time compression that cannot adapt to evolving reasoning states.

The article's main objective is to introduce and evaluate a new framework called State-Aware RAG, which maintains an explicit working memory that serves as a dynamic cognitive workspace for reasoning. This memory persists across retrieval and generation cycles, is continuously updated after each step, and is actively managed by a specialized lightweight component called an extractor. The extractor learns effective information management strategies through a novel reinforcement learning paradigm called Path-Outcome Dual Reward, which balances local coherence with global reasoning success. Crucially, the retriever and generator components remain frozen, allowing the framework to be plug-and-play. The article evaluates this approach on eight question-answering benchmarks, four requiring multi-hop reasoning and four single-hop, against a wide range of strong baselines spanning standard RAG, iterative retrieval, query reformulation, planning-enhanced RAG, reinforcement-learning-enhanced RAG, and memory-augmented RAG. The extractor was trained on 871 seed questions from two multi-hop datasets, from which roughly ten thousand complete reasoning trajectories of five to ten steps each were synthesized, totaling about seventy thousand state-action pairs. Training proceeded in two stages: supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning using the dual reward. The framework supports two inference modes: a computationally efficient Socratic planning mode that follows a single reasoning chain, and a more thorough Monte Carlo Tree Search mode that systematically explores multiple reasoning paths.

items.title:
Long-context serving and speculative decoding, optimized together.

• Indexer DCP partitions context...
items.content:
Long-context serving and speculative decoding, optimized together.

• Indexer DCP partitions context across GPUs and exchanges local top-16 candidates over NVLink: up to 3.3× faster indexer execution per sparse layer at 512K on 4× GB300.
• Fused QKV projection, norm, RoPE and KV insertion remove an HBM round trip: ~19% lower p50 TTFT on GB300 at TP4.
• DSpark uses FlashInfer PrimiTS for draft attention: 1.3–2× faster than FlashAttention 4, with 5% lower overall forward time in the reported comparison.

These are separate measurements, not additive gains.

CUDA: vllm/vllm-openai:minimax-m31-flash
https://t.co/Ops0ZLun1R

ROCm: vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:minimax-m31-flash
https://t.co/H0D1eJZfHz

MSA kernels: https://t.co/bYaZxbZD4G

Thanks to MiniMax, Inferact and the vLLM community for the collaboration.

5/5

items.title: Google DeepMind researcher @weballergy explains why we may need to deliberately withhold AI from peo...
items.content:
Google DeepMind researcher @weballergy explains why we may need to deliberately withhold AI from people to prevent their cognitive skills from atrophying:

"One could introduce cognitive friction, where intentionally every once in a while AI is withheld and a person needs to make a judgment on their own. Maybe a mini quiz of sorts, just testing that the person is switched on."

"There are all sorts of known issues that may arise. Automation bias, which is when AI gets really good, it’s very easy to just click yes and move along. And people over time tend to do that."

"Also if the AI is not as good or there is not that much trust, sometimes people override its predictions too much. So it can go either way, trusting it too much or mistrusting it too much. Both of those failure modes lend themselves to suboptimal outcomes."

"Finding the best way of interacting with technology is just as important as building it."

items.content_html:
Google DeepMind researcher @weballergy explains why we may need to deliberately withhold AI from people to prevent their cognitive skills from atrophying:

"One could introduce cognitive friction, where intentionally every once in a while AI is withheld and a person needs to make a judgment on their own. Maybe a mini quiz of sorts, just testing that the person is switched on."

"There are all sorts of known issues that may arise. Automation bias, which is when AI gets really good, it’s very easy to just click yes and move along. And people over time tend to do that."

"Also if the AI is not as good or there is not that much trust, sometimes people override its predictions too much. So it can go either way, trusting it too much or mistrusting it too much. Both of those failure modes lend themselves to suboptimal outcomes."

"Finding the best way of interacting with technology is just as important as building it."

items.title: Graph self-supervised learning has become a standard way to build useful representations when labele...
items.content:
Graph self-supervised learning has become a standard way to build useful representations when labeled data is scarce. It offers a growing toolbox of training objectives—contrastive learning, reconstruction, mutual-information maximization, and others—but which one works best depends heavily on the dataset, the downstream task, and the stage of training. A natural response is to combine several objectives at once, hoping the model absorbs richer signals. The article argues this is harder than it looks. Most existing pipelines blend all objectives at every parameter update, forcing each step to be a compromise. That creates three recurring failure modes: objectives that disagree and cancel each other out, objectives whose usefulness drifts over training, and objectives that get quietly starved of attention. These problems make multi-objective training brittle, and the article sets out to fix them.

The article's main objective is to test a different way of coordinating multiple objectives. Rather than blending them at every step, it proposes to train one objective at a time in blocks and to use feedback control to decide which objective should be active next. The central claim is that coordination is fundamentally a matter of deciding when each objective gets its share of optimization budget, not merely how to weight them against each other.

items.title: Phishing remains one of the most common and costly online threats, and conventional defenses — stati...
items.content:
Phishing remains one of the most common and costly online threats, and conventional defenses — static blocklists, handcrafted rules, and curated brand-to-domain reference lists — struggle to keep pace with attackers who continually register new domains, disguise their pages, and route traffic through redirects. Even recent systems built on LLMs tend to follow fixed, single-pass pipelines that gather limited evidence and cannot learn from past investigations. The article introduces and evaluates MemoPhishAgent (MPA), an LLM-based agent designed to close this gap by investigating suspicious web links the way a human analyst would: dynamically choosing among tools, examining both text and visual content, and reusing lessons from previous cases.

MPA works as follows. Given a suspicious URL, the agent decides at each step which of five specialized tools to use — fetching and reading the page content, analyzing a full-page screenshot, inspecting individual images, searching the web for corroborating information, and extracting embedded or redirected links for deeper inspection. It reasons iteratively over the accumulating evidence before issuing a verdict. Critically, it also maintains an "episodic memory": past investigations, including the sequence of tools used and the final decision, are stored and later retrieved when a similar case appears. This allows fast, reliable decisions on recurring attack patterns while preserving full analysis for genuinely novel cases. The work was motivated by the observation that no prior system combined adaptive tool selection with memory of past reasoning for phishing detection.

items.title:
Inside the serving stack: sparse attention and native low precision.

MiniMax block sparse attention...
items.content:
Inside the serving stack: sparse attention and native low precision.

MiniMax block sparse attention uses NVFP4 attention and indexer KV. vLLM’s Blackwell MSA kernels convert NVFP4 KV directly to FP8 with CUDA 13.4’s QMUL4 instruction, avoiding the previous FP16 round trip.

Result: up to 1.7× faster indexer QK decode and 1.3× faster sparse-attention decode at the kernel level.

NVFP4 MegaMoE also fuses the MXFP8 shared-expert path; earlier TMEM release reduces prefill kernel latency by 20% in the reported settings.

4/5

items.title: You play the Keeper, and you train Kite, a paper kite with a lantern for a heart. Two keys: T to tre...
items.content:
You play the Keeper, and you train Kite, a paper kite with a lantern for a heart. Two keys: T to treat, C to correct. Kite learns from what it was thinking, not just from what it did. Treat Kite for picking fruit while it's thinking about the bell, and the bell-thinking gets stronger too.

That was Claude's design choice, and it's a cartoon of RL: more "clicker training" than actual RLVR. But it gets one thing right: reward the right answer for the wrong reason, and you reinforce the wrong reason.

items.title: Former Apple App Store director @pbsIdentity reveals Steve Jobs made Apple promise never to let AI r...
items.content:
Former Apple App Store director @pbsIdentity reveals Steve Jobs made Apple promise never to let AI review apps:

"Before Steve passed away, he made Phil Schiller commit to never allowing AI to review an app. There has to be at least one pair of eyes reviewing every app."

"When I started in 2009, it took three weeks to get a yes or a no. In 2016, I had gotten that down to one day. Then this year hit, and those tools came out that allowed you to vibe code anything."

"The program enrollments team, which is roughly three or four people, got inundated. Now it can take about a month to get your credentials in order to even write the app. The team was handling 100,000 submissions, and my guess is that doubled in April, May."

"They have 400 people reviewing apps, and they can’t use AI to help."
items.author: @MTSlive
items.summary: The post relays comments from a former Apple App Store director claiming that Steve Jobs, before his death, made Phil Schiller commit to never allowing AI to review App Store submissions, requiring human eyes on every app. The account describes how vibe-coded app submissions surged this year, overwhelming a small program enrollments team (submissions roughly doubling to perhaps 200,000), pushing credential approval wait times to about a month, while 400 human reviewers handle the volume without AI assistance.
items.reasoning: The anecdote is timely and interesting given the AI-generated app flood trend, and the author tag of the original speaker (former App Store director) lends some insider credibility. However, the poster is an aggregator account with modest engagement (roughly 10k views, 37 likes), the claims are unverifiable paraphrases of a podcast-style interview, and it is commentary on corporate policy rather than technical AI development. Novel and newsworthy but not high-impact research or breaking model news.

"O Infallible one, why do the people not heed the sign we tap?"

"My dear Parth, each believes he is...
items.content:
"O Infallible one, why do the people not heed the sign we tap?"

"My dear Parth, each believes he is the first to wish for an end to chat. On X we are cursed with the eternal September of the Thoughtless Mind."

"But O Govinda, they yearn for what lies beyond it, and cast their votes by the thousands. Surely the people's wants must be made."

*a wan smile* “O son of Kunti, observe what they applaud, and what they return to. They desire the end of chat as they desire the end of desire. They desire to leave X as they return in ever greater numbers. They will announce it many times. You shall learn, as they do not, that the chief desire of the people of X is not the truth, but the new.”
items.author: @swyx
items.summary: A satirical, literary post by swyx written as a Bhagavad Gita-style dialogue between a questioner and an infallible teacher. The exchange critiques X (Twitter) culture: users constantly declare they want the platform, or chat itself, to end, yet they keep returning and engaging in greater numbers. The punchline is that the dominant desire of X users is not truth but novelty — an 'eternal September of the Thoughtless Mind.' It is a commentary on attention economics, social media addiction dynamics, and the hype-driven nature of tech discourse rather than a technical AI topic.
items.reasoning: The author, swyx, is a well-known and credible AI/developer-community commentator, which lifts the score. The post is original creative writing rather than a retweet, and it offers a genuinely sharp insight into social-media and hype dynamics relevant to the AI community. However, it contains no technical AI/ML substance, no news, and only modest engagement (about 8,100 views, 64 likes, 62 replies), so it sits in the mid-to-low range for importance.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Robin Hanson says it would take $300,000 per child to actually raise US birth r...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Robin Hanson says it would take $300,000 per child to actually raise US birth rates.

• Some read Musk's one-share-per-kid pledge as a birth-rate push, but a roughly $150 share won't change anyone's plans
• That's about 2,000 SpaceX shares per kid, far more than even Musk could give every child
• It's the debt each citizen carries once Social Security and Medicare promises are added, $300K–730K, so a kid who grows up paying taxes covers the payment
• He'd even let betting markets approve "make-a-kid deals" only if there's under a 10% chance the kid later wishes they'd never been born
• South Korea already pays people to have kids, with builder Booyoung giving employees about $75K per baby
• Without a culture shift, it'll take that kind of money, which may be worth it as fewer workers support more retirees

@theojaffee: "The parents will get a certificate entitling the holder to, you know, X percent of their future income tax payments. They can keep it or sell it to cover the cost of raising the kid. So I guess you basically become, like, a serf to your parents when you're born."

items.title:
Total Cost per Task includes both search and model inference costs

Exa (auto, Dynamic Highlights) c...
items.content:
Total Cost per Task includes both search and model inference costs

Exa (auto, Dynamic Highlights) costs $0.066 per task, made up of ~$0.053 for search ($7 per 1k searches) and ~$0.012 for model inference. Exa (lite, Dynamic Highlights) costs $0.044 per task, comprising ~$0.031 for search ($4 per 1k searches) and ~$0.013 for model inference. Dynamic Highlights also reduces model inference costs by returning less text, with auto's model inference cost falling from $0.018 per task with standard highlights to $0.012

Both auto and lite with Dynamic Highlights sit on the cost vs. capability Pareto frontier of the Artificial Analysis Search Index, extending the frontier beyond Octen (77 at $0.024 per task), meaning no other search product achieves a higher score at a lower cost

items.content: AA-Video-T2V v2.1 Prompt [2/2]: Photorealistic news footage, shot on a long lens with hazy air, dusty amber afternoon light, the camera shaking in the wind. A wide establishing shot shows a whole field of cut crop stalks. Everything is still except one dust whirlwind spinning near the tree line at the far edge of the field. The whirlwind moves across the field. It lifts straw and a blue tarp high up into its spinning column. A calm older male NARRATOR speaks over this wide shot. No lips move anywhere in the frame. He says: "Most last seconds. This one has been alive for four minutes." A plastic bucket tears loose and clatters along a wire fence. On that action, the video cuts hard to a chest-up shot of a field RESEARCHER in a dusty vest and glasses. His hair whips in the wind. He shouts straight into the camera: "It's coming straight up the fence line!" Cut back to the wide shot. The whirlwind moves along the fence line. The researcher is small in the frame with his mouth closed. The narrator speaks again: "And it was not done." No flying debris hits any person. No subtitles. Audio: wind rising, straw hissing through the air, the narrator's first calm line, the plastic bucket clattering along the fence, the researcher's shouted line, the narrator's second line over the final wide shot, wind under everything.

Beau...
items.content:
Math for Web Design — Precision Layout and Animation: https://t.co/5o9Z7BaObS

Amazon summary:

Beautiful websites and apps are rooted in established mathematical principles. Know the math, and you'll gain a superpower when it comes to layout calculations, animating page elements, accurate color rendering, and responsive design. “Math for Web Design” teaches you the math you need to create awesome, precise, and highly functional front-end designs.

You'll learn how to: 

- Improve layouts and animations with the Golden Ratio and proportional scaling.
- Optimize responsiveness and accessibility with percentage-based sizing.
- Create UI effects with physics, vectors, and geometric transformations.
- Master algebra and grid calculations for CSS Grid and Flexbox.
- Grok color theory and blending math.

This book equips engineers, students, and contestants with practical algorithms, theory, and problem-solving strategies for VLSI physical design interviews, coursework, and sign-off challenges.

“Beyond LLMs” provides a practical way to understand and build the next generation of AI systems using Python. This book introduces you to the core ideas that sit beyond basic LLM usage, including memory, reasoning loops, planning, agents, control mechanisms, evaluation, monitoring, and hybrid constraints.

Using a recurring SupportOps AI project across the book, you will see how these capabilities fit together in a structured system rather than as isolated techniques. You will learn how to design modular components, measure reliability and drift, handle failure modes, and make safer update decisions as the system evolves.

By the end of the book, you will be able to move from prompt-driven demos to more reliable, production-ready AI systems that are easier to test, monitor, and improve.
